items.boundary: Would an n=2→n=2 transition yield a spectral line?
items.boundaryAnswer: No. Its level-energy difference is zero; the line formula yields zero wavenumber, not a finite emitted photon.
items.challenge: Independently find λ(5→2)/λ(4→2) for a hydrogen-like atom. Show the inverse-ratio logic; numerical R is unnecessary.
items.concept: Hydrogenic emission uses 1/λ = R(1/n_low²−1/n_high²). A larger energy or wavenumber gap means a shorter wavelength; always choose n_high greater than n_low.
items.predict: Will the 4→2 Balmer photon have a shorter or longer wavelength than the 3→2 photon? Predict before evaluating fractions.
items.repair: Write each wavenumber factor, put λ proportional to its reciprocal, then compare the resulting ratio and inequality.
steps: Compute the 5→2 wavenumber factor: 1/4−1/25=21/100.
For 4→2 the factor is 3/16. Invert factors for wavelengths: λ(5→2)/λ(4→2)=(3/16)/(21/100)=25/28≈0.893.
The 5→2 transition emits the shorter wavelength because its level gap is larger.
items.subject: CHEMISTRY
items.title: Atomic spectra: inverses, not energy gaps
items.trap: Using the ratio of energy gaps as though it were the ratio of wavelengths.

items.boundary: If oxygen supplied were only 20 mL for 12 mL methane, could all methane burn completely?
items.boundaryAnswer: No. Complete combustion needs 24 mL oxygen; the mixture is oxygen-limited and cannot be evaluated with the all-methane-complete assumption.
items.challenge: Burn 12 mL CH4 with 30 mL O2 at the same gas conditions. Determine the dry volume after water condenses and the final volume after removing CO2 with alkali.
items.concept: At the same temperature and pressure, gas volumes follow stoichiometric mole ratios. In CH4 + 2O2 → CO2 + 2H2O, water is condensed before reading the dry gas; an alkali absorbent can then remove CO2.
items.predict: After burning methane in excess oxygen and condensing water, is the remaining dry gas necessarily only carbon dioxide?
items.repair: Write three separate columns: reacted volume, dry gas after condensation, and gas after selective CO2 absorption.
steps: Required O2 is twice methane: 24 mL, leaving 30−24=6 mL O2.
CO2 formed is 12 mL; after condensing water, dry volume =12+6=18 mL.
An alkaline absorber removes 12 mL CO2, leaving 6 mL O2.
items.subject: CHEMISTRY
items.title: Gas-volume conservation in combustion eudiometry
items.trap: Counting water vapour as dry gas or subtracting CO2 before calculating oxygen excess.
items.worked: 15 mL CH4 consumes 30 mL O2, leaving 5 mL from an initial 35 mL O2. It produces 15 mL CO2: dry residual gas =20 mL; after CO2 absorption, 5 mL remains.

items.boundary: Would the same simple partial-pressure rule remain valid if gases react appreciably before measurement?
items.boundaryAnswer: Not with the initial unreacted mole numbers. First determine equilibrium compositions; only then use the relevant mixture relations.
items.challenge: A 10-atm ideal mixture contains 1 mol helium and 4 mol neon. Calculate each partial pressure, then check whether they sum to total pressure.
items.concept: For an ideal nonreacting gas mixture at equilibrium, Dalton's law is p_i = x_i P_total, where x_i=n_i/Σn. Mole fractions must sum to one.
items.predict: Can a minority gas by mole count have a larger partial pressure than a majority gas under identical ideal mixing conditions?
items.repair: Find the total moles first, then normalize each component amount before multiplying by total pressure.
steps: Total moles are 1+4=5; x_He=1/5 and x_Ne=4/5.
Apply Dalton's law: p_He=(1/5)×10=2 atm and p_Ne=(4/5)×10=8 atm.
Check p_He+p_Ne=10 atm; each partial pressure is nonnegative and ≤ total.
items.subject: CHEMISTRY
items.title: Mole fraction and partial pressures
items.trap: Using molar mass or an arbitrary volume fraction when the ideal mixture is specified by mole numbers.
items.worked: In a vessel with 2 mol N2 and 3 mol O2 at total pressure 5 atm, x_N2=2/5 and x_O2=3/5, yielding p_N2=2 atm and p_O2=3 atm.

items.boundary: If only 0.10 mol HCl is available for this 8.14 g sample, can all of the ZnO dissolve?
items.boundaryAnswer: No. Only 0.050 mol ZnO can react with 0.10 mol HCl; the remaining 0.050 mol ZnO is unreacted under this acid-only model.
items.challenge: A clean 8.14 g sample of ZnO reacts with HCl. Calculate the minimum amount of HCl in moles and the volume of 0.50 M HCl solution needed.
items.concept: Amphoteric ZnO reacts with both acid and excess strong alkali. Balance the atoms and charge before applying a mole ratio. With acid, ZnO + 2HCl → ZnCl2 + H2O.
items.predict: Would adding twice as many moles of HCl as ZnO be sufficient for complete acid dissolution? State the stoichiometric reason.
items.repair: Mark the coefficient 2 in the balanced reaction and write mole-needed = coefficient × limiting-reactant moles.
steps: n(ZnO)=8.14/81.4=0.100 mol, using the molar mass of ZnO and the measured sample mass.
The balanced equation needs 2 mol HCl per mol ZnO, hence n(HCl)=0.200 mol.
items.subject: CHEMISTRY
items.title: Amphoteric oxides and equivalent bookkeeping
items.trap: Using a 1:1 ratio because the oxide formula contains one zinc atom.
items.worked: 4.07 g of ZnO at molar mass 81.4 g/mol is 0.050 mol. Its acid dissolution needs 0.100 mol HCl, not 0.050 mol.

items.boundary: Would the same five-electron permanganate reduction necessarily apply in strongly alkaline solution?
items.boundaryAnswer: No. The Mn product and electron stoichiometry depend on medium; confirm the reaction product and rebalance for that environment.
items.challenge: 25.0 mL of 0.0100 M acidic KMnO4 reaches the equivalence point with Fe²⁺. Determine the Fe²⁺ amount in moles and the 0.0500 M Fe²⁺ solution volume consumed.
items.concept: In acidic solution, MnO4− takes 5 electrons to become Mn²⁺, whereas Fe²⁺ donates one electron to become Fe³⁺. Balance exchanged electron-moles before titration arithmetic.
items.predict: Does one mole of acidic permanganate oxidise one mole or five moles of Fe²⁺? Explain the electron count.
items.repair: Balance the oxidation/reduction half-reactions first and then use n oxidant×n-factor = n reductant×n-factor.
steps: Five Fe²⁺ donate the five electrons needed per permanganate; n(Fe²⁺)=1.25×10⁻³ mol.
items.subject: CHEMISTRY
items.title: Redox titration by electron-equivalent balance
items.trap: Assuming a one-to-one mole ratio without considering the oxidation-state changes.
items.worked: 20 mL of 0.020 M KMnO4 contains 0.00040 mol permanganate and can oxidise 5×0.00040=0.00200 mol Fe²⁺ in acid.

items.boundary: Would the same 5R/6 expression hold for two adjacent cube vertices?
items.boundaryAnswer: No. For adjacent vertices the symmetry grouping changes; the known equal-resistor cube value is 7R/12.
items.challenge: Every edge of a cube is 6 Ω. Find the equivalent resistance between opposite body-diagonal vertices and show the three symmetry reductions.
items.concept: For twelve equal edge resistors R in a cube, opposite-corner terminals produce two groups of three equipotential near vertices. Replace edges between each group with parallel equivalents.
items.predict: Between opposite cube corners, will three near vertices have the same potential?
items.repair: Use automorphisms of the cube that leave source terminals fixed to identify equal-potential vertices before circuit reduction.
steps: At each terminal, three equal outgoing resistors are parallel: 6/3=2 Ω.
Between the two groups of three same-potential nodes are six 6 Ω edges in parallel: 6/6=1 Ω.
The three stages are series-connected: 2+1+2=5 Ω.
items.subject: PHYSICS
items.title: Cube networks by equipotential groups
items.trap: Treating the twelve edges as identical paths from terminal to terminal without grouping equipotential nodes.
items.worked: For a body diagonal, the three entrance edges are R/3, the six middle edges R/6, and the three exit edges R/3; R_eq=5R/6.

items.boundary: What is the input resistance of one cell consisting only of a series R followed by its terminal shunt R?
items.boundaryAnswer: It is 2R for the stated one-cell termination, greater than the infinite-tail limit φR; a finite ladder must specify its termination.
items.challenge: Each series and shunt resistor of a self-similar infinite ladder is 4 Ω. Find input resistance to three significant figures and exclude the nonphysical quadratic root.
items.concept: An infinite resistor ladder is identical to its tail. If each cell has a series R followed by a shunt R in parallel with the remaining ladder X, X=R+R X/(R+X).
items.predict: Does adding one more identical cell change the input resistance of an already infinite self-similar ladder?
items.repair: Define exactly what is repeated, derive the self-similarity equation, and apply a passive-resistance sign check.
steps: Write X=4+(4X)/(4+X); multiply by (4+X).
Simplify to X²−4X−16=0, giving X=2(1±√5).
Choose positive X=2(1+√5)=6.472 Ω; negative resistance is not passive.
items.subject: PHYSICS
items.title: Infinite ladders and self-consistency
items.trap: Solving the quadratic but retaining its negative root, or treating the entire infinite network as a finite two-resistor cell.
items.worked: Rearrange X=R+RX/(R+X) to X²−RX−R²=0. The physically positive root is X=φR with φ=(1+√5)/2.

items.boundary: If the resistor connecting the two equipotential middle vertices is removed, does the equivalent resistance change?
items.boundaryAnswer: No, while the remaining resistor values preserve that symmetry. The removed resistor had zero current.
items.challenge: Six 12 Ω resistors form the six edges of a tetrahedron. Find equivalent resistance between any two vertices and explain why no source current uses the opposite connecting edge.
items.concept: In a symmetric K4 network of six identical resistors R, the two vertices not used as terminals have equal potential. No current passes through their joining edge.
items.predict: If voltage is applied between two K4 vertices, do the other two vertices have equal or different potentials?
items.repair: Label terminals and symmetry-equivalent nodes, then reduce series and parallel branches only after checking their current paths.
steps: Exchange the remaining two vertices while leaving the terminals fixed: the network is unchanged, so their potentials are equal.
Their joining 12 Ω edge has zero voltage drop; the two two-edge routes each total 24 Ω and combine to 12 Ω.
The direct 12 Ω edge parallels this 12 Ω combination, giving 6 Ω.
items.subject: PHYSICS
items.title: A tetrahedron of resistors
items.trap: Adding all six resistors in series or discarding the direct-edge branch.
items.worked: Delete the zero-current cross-edge by symmetry. The two side routes each have 2R and are in parallel, giving R, which is parallel to the direct edge R; R_eq=R/2.

items.boundary: With identical charges fixed, what happens to the force if the separation is doubled?
items.challenge: Keep r=0.03 m but raise equal-charge repulsion to 0.004 N. Estimate the magnitude of each charge and the number of elementary charges (e=1.6×10⁻¹⁹ C).
items.concept: For two identical point charges separated by r, F=kq²/r². Solve q from the square root and estimate N=|q|/e, checking integer charge quantization and orders of magnitude.
items.predict: At fixed separation, if measured repulsion becomes four times as large, will each equal charge double or quadruple?
items.repair: Isolate q² before taking the positive square root for magnitude, then divide by e and check units.
steps: The force quadruples at fixed r, so |q| doubles to 2.0×10⁻⁸ C.
N=q/e=(2.0×10⁻⁸)/(1.6×10⁻¹⁹)=1.25×10¹¹ elementary charges, using the magnitude of each electron's charge.
The count is enormous but compatible with charge quantization; only the sign must be chosen from attraction/repulsion information.
items.subject: PHYSICS
items.title: Coulomb force and electron-count scale
items.trap: Replacing q² with q or overlooking the square root when inverting Coulomb's law.
items.worked: For r=0.03 m, F=0.001 N, k=9×10⁹, the equal charge is q=√(F r²/k)=1.0×10⁻⁸ C.

items.boundary: Under a small-angle model, how does the exit slope magnitude vary when v₀ doubles?
items.boundaryAnswer: The exit slope is |q|EL/(mv₀²), so it too falls to one-quarter while E and L remain fixed.
items.challenge: A charged particle deflects by 8.0 mm in a uniform transverse plate field. With field strength and plate length fixed, how much does it deflect if its entry speed is doubled? State direction separately.
items.concept: A charge entering a uniform transverse electric field with horizontal speed v₀ has transit time t=L/v₀, transverse acceleration a=qE/m, and displacement magnitude |y|=|q|E L²/(2mv₀²).
items.predict: If the entry speed doubles while field and plate length stay fixed, does the deflection fall by a factor of two or four?
items.repair: Start from the x-flight time and y-acceleration, then retain both the t² factor and the charge sign.
steps: Transit time halves because t=L/v₀ when the field region has a fixed horizontal length L.
Electric transverse acceleration magnitude is unchanged, but y=(1/2)at² so the deflection falls by factor four.
The new displacement magnitude is 8.0/4=2.0 mm. Its direction is set by the sign of q and field orientation.
items.subject: PHYSICS
items.title: Transverse electrostatic deflection
items.trap: Using y∝t, forgetting the squared time, or identifying force direction without charge sign.
items.worked: The speed dependence is v₀⁻²: at unchanged field and length, twice v₀ gives one-quarter the deflection.

items.boundary: If the approaching south pole instead moves away, does induced current reverse?
items.boundaryAnswer: Yes, for the same orientation and nonzero motion: the sign of flux change reverses and the induced current reverses.
items.challenge: A south pole is moved toward a conducting loop. Viewed from the magnet side, what is the induced current sense and which magnetic pole appears on the loop's near face?
items.concept: An induced current produces a magnetic field opposing the CHANGE in magnetic flux. For a bar magnet viewed from its approaching face, a north pole approaching a loop makes the near face of the loop a north pole.
items.predict: When a north pole approaches a conducting loop, should the loop attract it or repel the change in approach?
items.repair: Write flux direction and its time-change sign; select the opposing induced field, then apply the right-hand rule.
steps: An approaching south pole increases the flux associated with that approach.
To oppose the increased flux, the loop presents a south pole toward the approaching south pole.
A south face has clockwise current as seen from that face.
items.subject: PHYSICS
items.title: Lenz's law: identify flux change first
items.trap: Choosing current sense from the pole alone without deciding whether flux is increasing or decreasing.
items.worked: The near face of the loop must become north to oppose increasing north-pole flux; viewed from that magnet side the induced current is counterclockwise by the right-hand grip rule.

items.boundary: If resistance doubles in this ideal model, what happens to terminal speed?
items.boundaryAnswer: It doubles, since the magnetic drag coefficient is inversely proportional to R; this assumes all other effects remain negligible.
items.challenge: A similar frictionless rod has mass 0.010 kg while g, R, B and l retain their values. Compute terminal speed and thermal dissipation at that speed.
items.concept: For an ideal conducting rod of length l sliding across rails in magnetic field B with circuit resistance R, induced EMF=Blv, current=Blv/R and magnetic drag=B²l²v/R. Terminal speed obeys mg=B²l²v/R.
items.predict: If the circuit resistance doubles with everything else fixed, does magnetic braking strengthen or weaken at a given velocity?
items.repair: Derive induced current from EMF, multiply by Bl to obtain drag, and check mgv=I²R at terminal speed.
steps: At terminal speed, P_gravity=mgv=0.010×10×0.4=0.040 W.
Current is Blv/R=0.5×1×0.4/1=0.20 A, so I²R=0.040 W, confirming power balance.
items.subject: PHYSICS
items.title: Falling conductive rod: terminal magnetic damping
items.trap: Writing magnetic force proportional to B instead of B², or treating a terminal-speed balance as accelerating motion.
items.worked: With m=0.020 kg, g=10 m/s², R=1 Ω, B=0.5 T and l=1 m, v_term=mgR/(B²l²)=0.8 m/s.

items.boundary: Does endpoint averaging still determine displacement if velocity is curved rather than linear in time?
items.boundaryAnswer: Not in general. Use the actual integral of velocity versus time; equal endpoints can hide differing interior motion.
items.challenge: A cart accelerates uniformly in a straight line from +4 to +20 m/s over 6 s. Find displacement, average velocity and acceleration, showing the time-area connection.
items.concept: For constant acceleration in one dimension, v(t) is linear and average velocity equals the mean of initial and final velocities: v̄=(v₀+v_f)/2. Distance and displacement may differ if direction reverses.
items.predict: Is the midpoint-of-endpoint-velocities formula always valid for an arbitrary velocity-time curve?
items.repair: Sketch the actual v–t graph, integrate signed area, and check whether the linear-v assumption holds.
steps: Average velocity is (4+20)/2=12 m/s because the acceleration is constant throughout the interval.
Displacement is area under the trapezoidal v–t plot: 12×6=72 m.
Acceleration is (20−4)/6=8/3 m/s², equal to the uniform slope of the velocity-time graph.
items.subject: PHYSICS
items.title: Position, displacement and average speed
items.trap: Using the average-speed formula from the end speeds even when acceleration is nonuniform or the cart reverses.
items.worked: For constant acceleration from 3 to 15 m/s without reversal, the average velocity is 9 m/s regardless of the elapsed time.

items.boundary: What happens algebraically if u₁=f/2 in this relation?
items.boundaryAnswer: Then 1/u₂=2/f−2/f=0, so u₂ tends to infinity, not an additional finite position.
items.challenge: In the same stated algebraic relation let f=15 cm and u₁=30 cm. Find u₂, then explain what additional physical data are needed before calling both positions real.
items.concept: For a prescribed algebraic conjugate relation 1/u₁+1/u₂=2/f, distances must be solved with consistent sign conventions. A positive number below f may represent a virtual-image branch; it must not silently be called a real screen position.
items.predict: Can algebraic positive solutions below the focal length always be interpreted as real images on a screen?
items.repair: Separate the algebraic relation from the signed physical image equation; validate each root against the apparatus.
steps: Invert the algebraic equation to get u₂=10 cm, then keep physical image interpretation separate until signs and geometry are established.
Because 10 cm<f, an ordinary converging-lens real-image assumption is not sufficient; clarify geometry and sign conventions.
items.subject: PHYSICS
items.title: Coupled conjugate-distance constraints
items.trap: Equating any positive root with a real image or mixing virtual-object and real-object sign conventions.
items.worked: With f=12 cm and u₁=18 cm, 1/u₂=2/12−1/18=1/9, so u₂=9 cm. Interpret the branch using actual optics geometry.

items.boundary: As u tends to minus infinity, where does the convex mirror image form?
items.boundaryAnswer: The virtual image tends to v=f behind the mirror, while magnification tends to zero.
items.challenge: A convex mirror has focal length +10 cm and an object 20 cm in front. Compute virtual-image distance and magnification using a consistent sign convention.
items.concept: With Cartesian mirror signs, a real object has u<0 and a convex mirror has f>0. The equation 1/f=1/v+1/u gives a positive virtual image v between pole and focus.
items.predict: As an object moves farther from a convex mirror, does its virtual image approach the pole or the focus?
items.repair: Record the sign convention alongside each u, f and v, then check the known virtual/diminished behavior.
steps: Thus v=20/3≈6.67 cm, positive behind the mirror.
Magnification m=−v/u=+(20/3)/20=1/3: virtual, erect, diminished.
items.subject: PHYSICS
items.title: Convex mirrors: sign and limiting image position
items.trap: Giving the image a negative sign or using f<0 from a different sign convention without changing the equations.
items.worked: For f=15 cm and u=−30 cm, 1/v=1/15+1/30=1/10, hence v=10 cm behind the mirror.

items.boundary: If a point lies exactly in the mirror plane, where is its reflected image?
items.boundaryAnswer: It coincides with that plane: x_ref=2x_M−x_M=x_M.
items.challenge: A converging lens at x=0 has f=12 cm and an object 36 cm left of it. A plane mirror stands at x=30 cm. Find the lens's first image coordinate and its plane-mirror image coordinate; stop before any lens return pass.
items.concept: A thin converging lens with positive object-distance magnitude u>f has image distance v=fu/(u−f). A plane mirror at position x_M forms an image of a point at x at x_ref=2x_M−x. Any additional return pass through the lens needs a separate equation.
items.predict: Can a plane mirror image coordinate be found simply by reflecting the image point across the mirror plane?
items.repair: Label each optical element and intermediate image in a common coordinate system, then solve one propagation stage at a time.
steps: The lens first-image magnitude is v=fu/(u−f)=12×36/(36−12)=18 cm to the right.
Reflect x=18 cm across mirror x_M=30 cm: x_ref=2×30−18=42 cm.
The 42 cm coordinate is a plane-mirror virtual image; a subsequent return through the lens requires fresh ray tracing.
items.subject: PHYSICS
items.title: Lens image followed by plane-mirror reflection
items.trap: Multiplying two magnifications or double-counting the reflected path before defining the intermediate image and mirror coordinates.
items.worked: For lens f=10 cm and object u=30 cm, the intermediate lens image is v=15 cm. A plane mirror at x_M=20 cm reflects that point to coordinate 2×20−15=25 cm.

items.boundary: What angle does the same constrained model produce when n=1?
items.boundaryAnswer: A=180°/(2×1+1)=60°, consistent with its single-index anchor.
items.challenge: Use the same (2n+1)A=180° model with n=4. Compute A and compare with the n=2 model, stating the geometry assumption.
items.concept: In a particular ideal symmetric silvered-prism repeat path, the permitted apex angles satisfy (2n+1)A=180°, with integer reflection index n≥1. The relation is geometry-specific, not a universal prism law.
items.predict: Within this constrained model, do more internal reflections require a larger or smaller apex angle?
items.repair: State the ideal symmetric multi-reflection geometry and define n before using the closure relation.
steps: The angular closure factor is 2×4+1=9 for the n=4 member of the specified symmetric reflection family.
Therefore A=180°/9=20° from this constrained geometry, not from a universal prism refraction formula.
20°<36°: more repeat reflections correspond to smaller apex angle in this idealized family.
items.subject: PHYSICS
items.title: Silvered prisms: discrete reflection geometry
items.trap: Treating A=180/(2n+1) as a general refraction law valid for arbitrary prisms and ray paths.
items.worked: For n=2, the recurrence gives A=180°/5=36°. For n=3, A=180°/7≈25.71°.

items.boundary: If initial and final magnification magnitudes are identical, how many turns are needed in this model?
items.boundaryAnswer: Zero, provided the system stays on the same physical branch and no other adjustment is required.
items.challenge: A lens of focal length 12 cm changes magnification magnitude from 3 to 1 in the same arrangement. A screw moves 0.4 cm per turn. Find the lens travel and the required number of full turns.
items.concept: For a fixed-focus thin lens in the chosen real-image geometry, |u|=f(1+1/|m|). A screw of pitch p moves the lens by p per full turn. Thus turns N=|Δu|/p; confirm the two image states share the same geometry.
items.predict: If pitch is halved for the same required lens displacement, does turn count halve or double?
items.repair: Compute physical lens positions from each magnification before subtracting; then convert travel to turns using pitch as distance per rotation.
steps: The travel is |24−16|=8 cm between the two lens positions in the same assumed imaging branch.
At 0.4 cm per turn, N=8/0.4=20 full screw revolutions, with the pitch measured in cm per turn.
items.subject: PHYSICS
items.title: Lens magnification and screw pitch
items.trap: Multiplying by screw pitch instead of dividing or mistaking magnification magnitude for its reciprocal.
items.worked: With f=10 cm, magnification magnitudes 2 and 1, the displacement is |10(1/1−1/2)|=5 cm. At pitch 0.5 cm/turn, it takes 10 turns.
